topicDisplay: Changing Relations: Northern Ireland & its Neighbours 1920-49

learningObjectives.title: Partition and the creation of Northern Ireland
Politics and society in Northern Ireland
The impact of the Second World War

questions.q: Which Act of Parliament partitioned Ireland and provided for the creation of Northern Ireland?
options: The Government of Ireland Act 1920
The Anglo-Irish Treaty 1921
The Home Rule Act 1914
The Act of Union 1801
questions.explain: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned Ireland, establishing separate parliaments for Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland.

questions.q: How many of Ulster's counties were included in the new Northern Ireland?
options: Six
Nine
Four
Twenty-six
questions.explain: Northern Ireland was made up of six counties: Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry and Tyrone.

questions.q: Who became the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland?
options: James Craig
Edward Carson
Basil Brooke
Éamon de Valera
questions.explain: James Craig (later Lord Craigavon) served as Northern Ireland's first Prime Minister from 1921 until his death in 1940.

questions.q: Who formally opened the new Northern Ireland Parliament in Belfast in June 1921?
options: King George V
Prime Minister Lloyd George
King Edward VIII
James Craig
questions.explain: King George V opened the first Northern Ireland Parliament in Belfast City Hall in June 1921, appealing for peace and reconciliation.

questions.q: Why did the Boundary Commission of 1924-25 ultimately leave the border unchanged?
options: Its report was leaked and then suppressed, and the three governments agreed to keep the existing border
The Free State successfully gained Fermanagh and Tyrone
Britain refused to allow any commission to meet
A referendum in the border counties rejected any change
questions.explain: When a leak revealed the Commission proposed only minor changes, the report was suppressed and in 1925 the three governments agreed to retain the existing border.

questions.q: The Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921 affected the situation in Ireland by:
options: Creating the Irish Free State as a dominion, while Northern Ireland was allowed to opt out
Abolishing the Northern Ireland Parliament
Uniting all thirty-two counties under Dublin
Restoring direct rule from London over the whole island
questions.explain: The 1921 Treaty established the Irish Free State as a self-governing dominion, and Northern Ireland exercised its right to opt out and remain in the United Kingdom.

questions.q: Many nationalists in the six counties objected to partition mainly because:
options: They wanted a united, independent Ireland and now formed a large minority within Northern Ireland
They wished to remain fully within the United Kingdom
They preferred rule directly from London
They supported the Ulster Unionist Party
questions.explain: Nationalists opposed partition because they sought a united independent Ireland and found themselves a substantial minority under a Unionist-controlled government.

questions.q: Which piece of legislation gave the Northern Ireland government wide-ranging powers of arrest, detention and search from 1922?
options: The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act
The Government of Ireland Act
The Public Order Act
The Franchise Act
questions.explain: The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act 1922 gave the government sweeping powers, including internment without trial, and was renewed repeatedly.

questions.q: The armed reserve police force set up to support the RUC, whose most controversial section was widely resented by nationalists, was known as the:
options: Ulster Special Constabulary (the 'B Specials')
Royal Irish Constabulary
Ulster Volunteer Force
Irish Republican Army
questions.explain: The Ulster Special Constabulary, especially the part-time 'B Specials', was overwhelmingly Protestant and deeply mistrusted by the nationalist community.

questions.q: In 1932 the Northern Ireland Parliament moved into a grand new building on the outskirts of Belfast known as:
options: Stormont
Leinster House
Belfast City Hall
Dublin Castle
questions.explain: The Parliament Buildings at Stormont were officially opened in 1932, giving Northern Ireland's government its long-term home.

questions.q: Why did the Unionist government abolish proportional representation for local and later parliamentary elections in the 1920s?
options: To strengthen Unionist control and reduce the representation of nationalists and smaller parties
To make elections fairer for the Catholic minority
Because Britain ordered them to do so
To encourage more political parties to form
questions.explain: Abolishing PR in favour of first-past-the-post helped consolidate Unionist dominance and weakened nationalist and minority representation.

questions.q: The practice of 'gerrymandering', seen most notably in Londonderry, involved:
options: Drawing electoral boundaries so that a nationalist majority returned a Unionist-controlled council
Giving extra votes to Catholic householders
Banning nationalists from standing for election
Holding elections only in Protestant areas
questions.explain: Gerrymandering redrew ward boundaries so that even where nationalists were a majority, as in Londonderry, Unionists controlled the council.

questions.q: Nationalists complained that the local government franchise was unfair mainly because:
options: Only ratepayers (property owners and their spouses) could vote, disadvantaging poorer, often Catholic, households
Only Protestants were legally allowed to vote
Voting was limited to people over the age of thirty
Women were completely barred from voting
questions.explain: The ratepayer franchise for local elections meant non-householders could not vote and some business owners had extra votes, disadvantaging poorer Catholic households.

questions.q: The Outdoor Relief riots in Belfast in 1932 were significant because:
options: Unemployed Protestant and Catholic workers protested together against poor relief, a rare moment of cross-community unity
They led to the fall of the Craigavon government
They were organised entirely by the Ulster Unionist Party
They ended discrimination in Northern Ireland
questions.explain: The 1932 Outdoor Relief riots saw Protestant and Catholic unemployed unite over inadequate relief, an unusual example of cross-community protest.

questions.q: Which industries were the traditional mainstays of the Northern Ireland economy in this period?
options: Shipbuilding, linen and agriculture
Coal mining and steel
Car manufacturing and electronics
Oil refining and banking
questions.explain: Northern Ireland's economy relied heavily on shipbuilding (Harland and Wolff), the linen industry and farming, all of which suffered in the inter-war depression.

questions.q: During which year did the devastating German air raids known as the Belfast Blitz take place?
questions.explain: The Belfast Blitz occurred in April and May 1941, with the Easter Tuesday raid of 15-16 April being especially destructive.

questions.q: Why did the German raid on Belfast in April 1941 cause such heavy loss of life?
options: Belfast was poorly defended with few anti-aircraft guns, searchlights or shelters
The city had been fully evacuated in advance
The bombers used only incendiary devices that caused no casualties
Belfast had the strongest defences in the United Kingdom
questions.explain: Belfast's weak air defences and lack of shelters left it badly exposed, and the April 1941 raid killed around 900 people, the highest toll outside London in a single night.

questions.q: After the worst Belfast raid, fire brigades crossed the border from Dublin to help. Which of the following best explains why this was notable?
options: Éire was officially neutral, so de Valera sending help across the border was a significant humanitarian gesture
Éire had declared war on Germany that week
The Dublin brigades were part of the British armed forces
Northern Ireland had refused all outside assistance
questions.explain: Despite Éire's official neutrality, de Valera sent fire brigades from Dublin and other towns to aid Belfast, a striking humanitarian gesture across the border.

questions.q: Why did the Éire government under Éamon de Valera remain neutral during the Second World War?
options: To assert Irish independence from Britain, though it quietly favoured the Allies in some ways
Because it had formally allied with Nazi Germany
Because Britain had ordered it to stay out of the war
Because Northern Ireland demanded Éire's neutrality
questions.explain: De Valera kept Éire neutral to demonstrate Irish sovereignty, although in practice the government showed some quiet sympathy towards the Allies.

questions.q: How did the Second World War affect Northern Ireland's economy?
options: It boosted industry and greatly reduced unemployment as shipyards, aircraft factories and farms met wartime demand
It caused the total collapse of shipbuilding and linen
It had no measurable effect on employment
It forced most factories to close permanently
questions.explain: Wartime demand for ships, aircraft and food revived Northern Ireland's industries and sharply cut the high unemployment of the 1930s.

questions.q: Unlike the rest of the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland during the war did NOT experience which of the following?
options: The introduction of military conscription
Rationing of food
Air raids on Belfast
The arrival of American troops
questions.explain: Conscription was not extended to Northern Ireland, largely because of fears of nationalist resistance and unrest.

questions.q: In January 1942 the first American troops to be based in Europe arrived in Northern Ireland. What does this best illustrate?
options: Northern Ireland's strategic importance to the Allied war effort in the Atlantic
That Éire had joined the Allies
That the war in Europe had already ended
That Northern Ireland was neutral in the war
questions.explain: The arrival of US forces in Northern Ireland in 1942 reflected its strategic value as a base for the Battle of the Atlantic and later operations.

questions.q: A local council allocates most new housing to Protestant families in a way that also helps keep control of the council. This is an example of which criticism of Northern Ireland's government in this period?
options: Discrimination linked to electoral advantage
Fair and equal treatment of both communities
Strict neutrality between the two communities
Direct rule imposed from London
questions.explain: Nationalists argued that housing was allocated to favour Protestants and, because the franchise was tied to housing, this also helped maintain Unionist electoral control.

questions.q: A Unionist in 1925 celebrates the outcome of the Boundary Commission. Their satisfaction is best explained by the fact that:
options: The border stayed exactly as it was, keeping the six counties within Northern Ireland
Fermanagh and Tyrone were transferred to the Free State
Northern Ireland was abolished
The whole of Ulster was united with the Free State
questions.explain: Unionists welcomed the 1925 settlement because it confirmed the existing border and secured all six counties within Northern Ireland.
